name: The Song of the Hoe — per-translation overlay glossary
description: Per-translation overlay glossary for The Song of the Hoe (ETCSL 5.5.4). Houses composition-specific entries; cross-corpus Sumerian foundational vocabulary (diĝir, abzu, me, nam, zi, du-lum, the DINGIR-prefix / sh-digraph / lacuna-bracket / proper-name / manuscript-variant conventions) lives in the central glossary at data-content/i18n/translation-glossary.json. The Editor pass (v1.0.0) populates the composition-singular cruxes.
scopeNote: v1.0.0 — first Editor pass. Adds the composition-singular cruxes: the whole-composition /al/ paronomasia convention (the defining feature of the hymn); the al (ĝišal) hoe lexeme and its dual mattock/brick-mould sense; the al-tar contextual pun-lexeme ('hoe-wielder' / 'construction-work'); Uzu-ea / Uzu-mua ('Where Flesh Came Forth / Grew'), the cosmic place of human emergence; Dur-an-ki ('bond of heaven and earth') and the bulug axis-peg; the saĝ nam-lu2-ulu3 + u3-šub brick-mould human-prototype; numun kalam-ma 'the seed of the Land' and the ki dar germination-of-humankind motif; the šu-giri17-ĝal2 hand-to-nose obeisance idiom (sibling of the central prostration entry); Ninmena as a birth-goddess epithet; Nunamnir as an Enlil epithet; and the technical al-initial catalogue nouns of vv 83-93. Cross-corpus reach to Enki and Ninmah, Atraḫasīs I, and Genesis 2:7 (ʾadam/ʾadamah) is documented in entry rationales and per-line commentary, never in the i18n.en text. All entries here are composition-singular or chapter-localized; cross-corpus Sumerian foundational vocabulary lives in the central glossary.

terms.literal: hoe (the noun al), punned through scores of unrelated /al/-bearing words
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL renders the meaning in English and appends the Sumerian pun-word in parentheses at each occurrence (e.g. 'daylight broke forth (aled)'); Jacobsen and Kramer note the pun in apparatus; Black et al. (2004) preserve the parenthetical-Sumerian convention.
terms.wohChoice: Render the English meaning and append the relevant Sumerian /al/ pun-word in parentheses at each pun (the ETCSL convention); the recurring noun is anchored as 'hoe (al)'. The whole pun-chain is documented once here and in the line-8 commentary; the verse text stays a defensible scholarly rendering and is NOT distorted to manufacture an English pun.
terms.rationale:
**The defining formal feature of The Song of the Hoe is its sustained /al/ paronomasia.** From line 8 onward the scribe threads the hoe-syllable Sumerian *al* through scores of grammatically-unrelated words: verbal prefixes (*al-e3* 'came forth', *al-du3-e* 'it built', *al-ĝa2-ĝa2* 'lays out / subdues', *al-gi4-gi4* 'roars', *al-lum-lum* 'makes thrive', *al-ḫul2-ḫul2* 'rejoice'), the lexicalised noun *al-tar* ('hoe-wielder / construction-work'), the verbal-idiom *al ... dug4* ('to desire'), and a closing catalogue of *al*-initial or *al*-adjacent technical nouns (*al-ti-ri2-gu7*, *dur10-al-lub*, *al-lu5-ḫab2*, *ma-al-tum*, *ma-a-a-al-tum*, *ar-gibil2*, *al-la-nu-um*, *ar-ga-nu-um*, *algameš*). The pun is **untranslatable in principle**: the English sense and the Sumerian sound cannot both be carried in the running text.

**The production glossary had no convention governing Sumerian paronomasia,** so this entry rules on it at project level. Four handling-options were weighed: (i) meaning-in-English + Sumerian pun-word in parentheses at each pun; (ii) meaning-only with the pun-chain documented once in commentary; (iii) meaning + italicised inline pun-words; (iv) typographic marking of the 'hoe (al)' anchor only. **The WoH translation adopts (i), the ETCSL convention** (Black, Cunningham, Robson, Zólyomi 2004; the ETCSL English of c.5.5.4 follows it throughout), because it is the standard for Sumerian texts going through the ETCSL pipeline, it keeps the apparatus auditable (the reader sees exactly which Sumerian word is being punned at each point), and it does not require distorting the English to fabricate a target-language pun. **Jeremy Black**, *Reading Sumerian Poetry* (1998), pp. 64-71, treats the hoe-hymn's paronomasia as the locus-classicus of Sumerian literary wordplay and notes that the device is *aetiological-encyclopedic*: the pun yokes the humble hoe to every domain of cosmos, cult, kingship, agriculture, death, and craft, so that the single syllable *al* threads creation through civilisation.

**Lens-discipline note.** The paronomasia is a documented philological feature of the Sumerian text; no WoH-distinctive synthesis is involved in the rendering-convention itself. The convention is *direct* (it is the consensus editorial practice, explicit in the source's sound-shape). The cosmological readings that the lens cares about (human emergence, divine-toil relief) are carried in the per-line commentary and in the dedicated content-entries below, not in this convention entry and not in the English text.

**Bibliography.** J. Black, *Reading Sumerian Poetry* (1998); J. Black, G. Cunningham, E. Robson, G. Zólyomi, *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004), pp. 308-312 (the hoe-hymn translation and notes); B. Alster, 'Interaction of Oral and Written Poetry in Early Mesopotamian Literature' (in *Mesopotamian Poetic Language*, 1992) on Sumerian wordplay; S. N. Kramer, *The Sumerians* (1963), pp. 219-220.

terms.partOfSpeech: noun (with ĝiš wood-determinative): hoe / mattock / pickaxe
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'hoe'; Jacobsen ('The Creation of the Pickax', in The Harps that Once 1987 pp. 332-334): 'pickax'; Kramer (Sumerian Mythology 1944): 'pickaxe'; Civil and the agricultural-realia scholarship: 'hoe / mattock'
terms.wohChoice: hoe (al) — preserving the ETCSL rendering; the dual mattock-and-brick-mould-tamping function (the same tool that digs the soil also tamps clay into the u3-šub brick-mould) documented here and surfaced at the line-19 and line-96 commentary.
terms.rationale:
**The *al* (ĝišal) is the hoe / mattock that the hymn personifies and praises.** The ĝiš wood-determinative marks it as a wooden-hafted implement; the tool is a single-handed digging-and-tamping mattock, distinct from the *apin* (seeder-plough, mentioned at line 14 as a comparandum for the hoe's blade) and from the *dusu* (the earth-carrying basket, its constant companion at lines 10 and 98). The rendering 'hoe' is the ETCSL standard and is uncontroversial as the tool's core sense; **Jacobsen** preferred 'pickax' (his title for the related composition-motif, *The Harps that Once* 1987, pp. 332-334), which captures the percussive digging-function but is not adopted here because 'hoe' is the consensus modern rendering and the agricultural-realia (Civil, *The Farmer's Instructions* 1994) supports the hoe / mattock identification.

**The dual function — digging tool AND brick-mould tamper — is the lexeme's load-bearing point for this composition.** The same *al* that 'sunders heaven from earth' (lines 4-5, figuratively), founds the E-kur (line 35), and clears weeds (lines 51, 104-106) is also the tool with which Enlil 'placed the first of humankind in the brick-mould' (*u3-šub*, line 19) and which the closing litany equates outright with the brick-mould: *^ĝišal u3-šub-ba* — 'the hoe is the brick-mould' (line 96). In Mesopotamian building-realia the mattock and the brick-mould are paired: the mattock digs and works the clay; the *u3-šub* (an open rectangular wooden frame) shapes it into mud-bricks (see **Moorey**, *Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries* 1994, pp. 302-307 on brick-manufacture). The hymn exploits this realia to make the hoe the instrument of *both* construction and human-creation — the human prototype is cast like a brick.

**Cross-corpus link to the clay-fashioning of humankind.** The hoe-and-brick-mould human-creation of this composition is a *technological* variant of the more widespread *clay-modelling* creation found in Enki and Ninmah (where Ninmah pinches humans from *im*, abzu-clay; see that overlay's `ama-inana-mother-goddesses-class-noun` and the central `du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus`) and in Atraḫasīs I (where Mami / Bēlet-ilī fashions humans from clay mixed with the slain god's blood). The brick-mould image specifically literalises the clay-creation as *moulded* rather than *hand-modelled* — humankind mass-produced in the matrix that makes bricks. The cross-corpus link is thematic and is documented in commentary; it is not asserted in the English text. See **Lambert-Millard**, *Atra-ḫasīs* (1969), pp. 56-60; **Bottéro-Kramer**, *Lorsque les dieux faisaient l'homme* (1989), pp. 502-510 (the hoe-hymn translation and the clay-creation comparanda).

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4; T. Jacobsen, *The Harps that Once* (1987); M. Civil, *The Farmer's Instructions* (1994); P. R. S. Moorey, *Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries* (1994); Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004), pp. 308-312.

terms.literal: hoe-work / the wielding of the hoe → (i) the one who wields the hoe; (ii) the work done with the hoe (construction)
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'hoe wielder (?)' at line 44 (marked uncertain), 'construction site / building project' elsewhere; Black et al.: 'the work of the hoe'
terms.wohChoice: Context-sensitive: 'hoe-wielder (al-tar)' at line 44 (an agent epithet of Nudimmud), 'construction-work (al-tar)' at lines 45, 47, 48, 54, 55, 57, 58, 60. The Sumerian pun-word is appended per the /al/ paronomasia convention.
terms.rationale:
***Al-tar* is a lexicalised /al/ pun that the hymn deploys as a noun in two distinct senses,** and the choice between them is context-driven rather than fixed — hence claim_type *inferred* (the line-44 agent-reading is flagged uncertain even by ETCSL). The compound is *al* ('hoe') + *tar*; because *tar* is also the verb 'to cut / decree' (the second half of the destiny-idiom *nam tar*), the form simultaneously evokes the hoe, the work of the hoe, and the decreeing wordplay that saturates the hymn.

**Sense (i), 'hoe-wielder', at line 44.** *al-tar lu2 zid-de3 en ^dnu-dim2-mud-e* — the token-gloss reads *al-tar* as an agent-noun, 'hoe-wielder', an epithet of Lord Nudimmud (Enki) as the builder of the Abzu. ETCSL marks the reading uncertain ('hoe wielder (?)'). The agent-reading is defensible (Sumerian forms agent-nouns by various means and the parallelism with *lu2 zid* 'the rightful man' supports a personal referent), but it is not secure.

**Sense (ii), 'construction-work / building-project', at lines 45, 47, 48, 54, 55, 57, 58, 60.** Here *al-tar* is an abstract / activity noun: *eridug^ki al-tar-ra* 'Eridug being chosen for the construction-work' (45); *^ĝišal-tar mu-da-an-gub* 'stood by her at the construction-work' (48, 54, 58); *ki-bal-a ^ĝišal-tar ba-an-gub* 'introduced the construction-work into the rebel land' (60). The activity-reading is the consensus and is well-supported by the recurring *gub* ('stand by, assist at') and *ba-an-dug4* ('ordered / commissioned') collocations.

**The WoH translation renders the two senses by context** and appends the Sumerian *al-tar* in parentheses at each occurrence per the paronomasia convention. This matches **Black et al.** (2004, pp. 309-310), who render 'the work of the hoe' for the activity-sense and flag the line-44 agent-reading. The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the line-44 agent-reading is genuinely uncertain and (b) the decision to split the lexeme by context, rather than render it uniformly, is an editorial reading of the syntax rather than a lexicon-fixed fact.

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4 token-glosses and English; Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004), pp. 308-312; for *tar* 'cut / decree' and the *nam tar* idiom see the central entry `nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus`.

terms.partOfSpeech: cosmic toponym (the manuscript variant names the place by its own etymology): flesh + came-forth / grew
terms.literal: 'Where Flesh Came Forth' (uzu 'flesh' + e3 'to come/go out') / 'Where Flesh Grew' (uzu 'flesh' + mu2 'to grow/sprout')
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: ''Where Flesh Came Forth' / 'Where Flesh Grew' (the name of a cosmic location)' (the name translated in running prose); Jacobsen: 'the Flesh-Producer'; Kramer notes the toponym as the place of human emergence at Nippur
terms.wohChoice: Transliterated toponym + parenthetical translation of the name: Uzu-ea ('Where Flesh Came Forth') / Uzu-mua ('Where Flesh Grew'); both manuscript readings preserved via the manuscript-variant convention. The toponym is NOT over-rendered (no 'where humans were manufactured' or similar lens-loaded gloss); the etymology is given as the manuscripts give it.
terms.rationale:
**Uzu-ea / Uzu-mua is the cosmic location where humankind first emerges in this composition** — and the place is named, self-glossing, by the very manuscript variant: *uzu-e3-a* 'Where Flesh Came Forth' (*uzu* 'flesh' + *e3* 'to come/go out') against *uzu-mu2-a* 'Where Flesh Grew' (*uzu* 'flesh' + *mu2* 'to grow/sprout'). Both readings agree that *uzu* ('flesh') is the matter from which humankind issues; they differ only on the verb of emergence (issuing-forth vs vegetal-growth). ETCSL translates the name in running prose and marks it 'the name of a cosmic location'; the WoH translation keeps the toponym transliterated and appends the translated etymology, matching the project's standing practice for self-glossing Sumerian toponyms (cf. Dur-an-ki, below).

**The location is Nippur's cosmic-emergence point.** Uzu-ea / Uzu-mua is associated in the Nippur cosmographic tradition with the spot — at or near Dur-an-ki (line 7), the 'bond of heaven and earth' — where the first humans broke through the ground after Enlil's hoe opened it. The motif is *chthonic-vegetal*: humankind sprouts from the soil like a plant (cf. *numun kalam-ma* 'the seed of the Land', line 3, and *ki ... dar* 'break through the soil', line 20). See **Jacobsen**, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976), pp. 112-113 on the Nippur emergence-of-humankind tradition; **Kramer**, *Sumerian Mythology* (1944/1961), pp. 72-73; **Black et al.** (2004), p. 309 and n.

**Cross-corpus link to the flesh / soil / clay creation-substance complex.** The Sumerian *uzu* ('flesh') as the human-emergence-substance sits alongside the *im* ('clay') of Enki and Ninmah and Atraḫasīs and the Hebrew creation-of-humankind from *ʿăp̄ār min-hā-ʾăḏāmâ* ('dust from the ground') at Genesis 2:7, where the human (*ʾāḏām*) is formed from and named for the ground (*ʾăḏāmâ*) — a name-and-substance pun structurally analogous to the *uzu*-named *Where-Flesh-Grew*. The Sumerian, Akkadian, and Hebrew accounts are not philologically cognate (the substances differ: flesh vs clay vs dust), but they share the ANE *humankind-from-the-earth-substance* pattern, and the Sumerian and Hebrew both *name the place or the creature for the substance* (Uzu-mua / ʾăḏāmâ). The cross-corpus comparison is documented in **Westermann**, *Genesis 1-11* (1984), pp. 199-207 (the *ʾāḏām / ʾăḏāmâ* wordplay and ANE comparanda), and **Lambert**, 'A New Look at the Babylonian Background of Genesis' (*JTS* 16, 1965). The comparison is held to the apparatus; it is NOT asserted in the English text.

**The claim_type is *inferred*.** The *uzu* = 'flesh' gloss and the toponym-translation are direct (the manuscripts self-gloss). What is *inferred* is the identification of Uzu-ea / Uzu-mua as *the* human-emergence place and its location at/near Dur-an-ki — a reading well-supported by the named scholarship but resting on the Nippur cosmographic tradition rather than on an explicit statement in this text. The cross-corpus comparison to Genesis 2:7 is *inferred* (a reasonable comparative reading), not direct.

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4; T. Jacobsen, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976); S. N. Kramer, *Sumerian Mythology* (1944/1961); C. Westermann, *Genesis 1-11* (1984); W. G. Lambert, *JTS* 16 (1965); Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004).

terms.partOfSpeech: cosmic toponym (dur 'bond/bond-rope' + an 'heaven' + ki 'earth') + common noun bulug ('peg / pin / boundary-stake / axis')
terms.literal: Dur-an-ki = 'Bond of Heaven and Earth'; bulug = 'peg / pin / boundary-marker' (here the cosmic axis-peg Enlil fixes)
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'Dur-an-ki' (preserved as toponym); 'the axis of the world' for bulug; Jacobsen: 'the bond of heaven and earth' / 'the (cosmic) pole'; Kramer: 'Duranki, the bond of heaven and earth' (Nippur's cult-name)
terms.wohChoice: Keep 'Dur-an-ki' transliterated (the etymology 'bond of heaven and earth' given in commentary); render bulug as 'the cosmic bond' in the verse text. Principal verb 'fixed' (la2); variant 'raised up' (il2) preserved via the manuscript-variant convention.
terms.rationale:
**Dur-an-ki, 'the Bond of Heaven and Earth', is the cult-name of Nippur** and the cosmological hinge-point where heaven and earth meet — the cosmic junction Enlil establishes at the moment of creation. The compound is *dur* ('bond, bond-rope, tie') + *an* ('heaven') + *ki* ('earth'). ETCSL preserves the toponym; the WoH translation does likewise and gives the etymology in commentary, matching the project's practice for self-meaningful Sumerian toponyms. Nippur as Dur-an-ki, the navel where the cosmos is tied together, is a fixture of Sumerian theology: **Jacobsen**, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976), pp. 100, 121; **Kramer**, *The Sumerians* (1963), pp. 118-119; **George**, *House Most High: The Temples of Ancient Mesopotamia* (1993), s.v. Dur-an-ki and E-kur.

**The *bulug* crux.** The noun *bulug* (token-glossed 'sharp object') has a semantic range — 'peg, pin, needle, boundary-stake, axis' — and the line admits three readings of what Enlil fixes at Dur-an-ki: (a) 'the cosmic bond / axis' (the world-axis or world-pole tying heaven to earth — ETCSL's 'the axis of the world'); (b) 'the boundary-peg / stake' (the marker that pegs the junction in place); (c) 'the pole / pin' in a more concrete sense. The WoH translation renders 'the cosmic bond' in the verse text — close to ETCSL's 'axis of the world' but tying it lexically to the Dur(-an-ki) 'bond' — and documents the peg / axis / stake alternatives in commentary. The reading is *inferred*: the cosmic-axis interpretation is the scholarly consensus but the precise sense of *bulug* here is not lexicon-fixed.

**The variant verb.** The principal witness has *nam-mi-in-la2* (*la2* 'to hang, suspend, fix'); variants have *nam-il2-e / nam-il2-la* (*il2* 'to raise, lift up'). 'Fixed / suspended' vs 'raised up' both describe the erection of the cosmic axis; the WoH translation leads with 'fixed' (principal) and preserves 'raised up' via the manuscript-variant convention. The two verbs are not in real tension (one suspends the axis, the other raises it); both belong to the establishing-the-world-axis image.

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4; T. Jacobsen, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976); S. N. Kramer, *The Sumerians* (1963); A. R. George, *House Most High* (1993); Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004), p. 309.

terms.partOfSpeech: construct phrase: head/first + humankind + brick-mould (the matrix in which the human prototype is cast)
terms.literal: the head / first (specimen) of humankind ... into the brick-mould
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'the first model of mankind in the brick mould'; Jacobsen: 'placed the vanguard of mankind in the brick-mould'; Kramer / Black et al.: 'set the first of humankind into the brick-mould'
terms.wohChoice: 'he placed the first of humankind in the brick-mould' — saĝ read as 'the first / foremost (specimen)'; nam-lu2-ulu3 governed by the central humankind entry; u3-šub rendered 'brick-mould'. The clay-prototype reading is documented in commentary, not loaded into the verse.
terms.rationale:
**This is the human-creation crux of the composition:** Enlil 'placed the *saĝ nam-lu2-ulu3* in the *u3-šub*' (line 19) — set the first of humankind into the brick-mould. Three lexemes carry the weight.

***saĝ* ('head').** The base sense is 'head', but in this construction it is read as 'the first / the foremost / the vanguard (specimen)' of humankind — the prototype or first-cast individual. ETCSL renders 'the first model'; Jacobsen 'the vanguard'. The 'first / foremost specimen' reading is adopted because the parallel at line 18A (*saĝ nu-ĝa2-ĝa2-de3*, 'to settle a head / the first') and the litany at line 96 (*^ĝišal saĝ ĝal2-la-am3*, 'the hoe is what made the head / first exist') confirm *saĝ* here as the inceptive-specimen of mankind, not the anatomical head. The reading is *inferred* (a defensible construal of *saĝ* in context, not its default lexical value).

***nam-lu2-ulu3* ('humankind')** is governed by the central entry `nam-lu2-ulu3-sumerian-humankind-cross-corpus` (applied in the chapter); not duplicated here.

***u3-šub* ('brick-mould')** is the open rectangular wooden frame in which wet clay is shaped into mud-bricks (Moorey, *Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries* 1994, pp. 304-307). That humankind is cast in the *brick-mould* literalises the clay-creation of humanity as a *moulding / mass-production* process: the first human is shaped like a brick, in the brick-maker's matrix. The image returns explicitly at line 96 (*^ĝišal u3-šub-ba* — 'the hoe is the brick-mould').

**Cross-corpus link to the clay-fashioning of humankind (Enki and Ninmah; Atraḫasīs I; Genesis 2:7).** The brick-mould prototype is a *technological* form of the ANE clay-creation of humankind: in Enki and Ninmah, Ninmah pinches humans from *im* (abzu-clay) over the apsû; in Atraḫasīs I (lines 210-230), Mami / Bēlet-ilī mixes clay with the blood of the slain god Wê-ila and the birth-goddesses nip off fourteen pieces; in Genesis 2:7, YHWH-Elohim forms *hā-ʾāḏām* from *ʿăp̄ār min-hā-ʾăḏāmâ* ('dust from the ground'). The Song of the Hoe's distinctive contribution is the *mould*: humankind is not hand-modelled but cast in the brick-frame, the same tool-complex (hoe + mould) that builds temples and cities. The cross-corpus comparison is *inferred* — a reasonable comparative reading of shared ANE creation-from-earth-substance motifs — and is documented in the line-19 commentary, NOT asserted in the English text. See **Lambert-Millard**, *Atra-ḫasīs* (1969), pp. 56-60; **Bottéro-Kramer**, *Lorsque les dieux faisaient l'homme* (1989), pp. 502-510; **Westermann**, *Genesis 1-11* (1984), pp. 199-207; **W. G. Lambert**, *JTS* 16 (1965).

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4; P. R. S. Moorey, *Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries* (1994); T. Jacobsen, *The Harps that Once* (1987), pp. 332-334; Lambert-Millard, *Atra-ḫasīs* (1969); Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004).

terms.partOfSpeech: construct phrase + verb: seed + of-the-Land; place/earth + to-split/break-through
terms.literal: the seed of the Land (= the human seed) ... breaks/splits through the ground
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'the human seed of the Land come up from the earth'; 'his Land started to break through the soil'; Jacobsen / Kramer: 'the seed of mankind sprouted from the earth'
terms.wohChoice: 'the seed of the Land' (numun) made to sprout from the earth (principal reading; variant 'from the shrine' eš3-ta preserved); 'his Land began to break up through the soil' (ki dar — the people pushing up like germinating plants). The plant-emergence-of-humankind image is documented in commentary, not surfaced as a lens-claim.
terms.rationale:
**The composition opens with humankind imagined as a *crop*: a seed that Enlil germinates and that breaks through the soil.** Two lexical strands carry the image.

***numun kalam-ma* ('the seed of the Land'), line 3.** *numun* ('seed') is the agricultural term; *kalam* ('the Land' = Sumer, its people) is governed by the central entry `kalam-ka-na-ag-the-land-cross-corpus` (applied). The phrase *numun kalam-ma* is the *human seed of the Land* — humankind conceived as the germinating seed-stock of Sumer. Enlil makes it 'sprout up from the {earth} {variant: shrine}': the principal witness has *ki-ta* ('from the earth', chthonic emergence), variants have *eš3-ta* ('from the shrine', cultic emergence). The WoH translation leads with 'earth' (the chthonic-germination reading, which the rest of the passage develops) and preserves 'shrine' via the manuscript-variant convention. The Translator's option of rendering *numun* as 'human seed' explicitly was considered and **declined** for the verse text: 'the seed of the Land' is closer to the Sumerian and lets the human-referent emerge from context rather than being spelled out — the humankind sense is carried in commentary.

***ki ... dar* ('break through the soil'), line 20.** The verb *dar* ('to split, break through') is used of the Land (*kalam*) breaking up through the ground toward Enlil — the people pushing up through the earth like sprouting plants. ETCSL: 'his Land started to break through the soil'. This is the defining *vegetal-emergence-of-humankind* image: humans germinate and erupt from the soil. The WoH translation renders 'his Land began to break up through the soil', preserving the people-as-the-agent-pushing-up reading.

**Cross-corpus link.** The seed-and-germination imagery for the origin of humankind connects to the *uzu-mua* ('Where Flesh Grew', *mu2* 'to sprout') toponym (lines 6, 18, 18A; see the dedicated entry) and, comparatively, to the Hebrew *ʾāḏām / ʾăḏāmâ* ground-and-human wordplay at Genesis 2:7 — though the Sumerian image is specifically *botanical* (humans as a sprouting crop) where the Hebrew is *plastic* (the human moulded from dust). The comparison is *inferred* and is held to commentary. See **Jacobsen**, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976), pp. 112-113; **Westermann**, *Genesis 1-11* (1984), pp. 199-207; **Black et al.** (2004), pp. 308-309.

**The claim_type is *inferred*.** That *numun* = 'seed' and *dar* = 'break through' is direct; that the passage portrays *humankind* germinating from the soil is a reading (well-supported, consensus) that rests on construing *kalam* / the unstated subject as the human-collective, and the cross-corpus comparison is a reasonable comparative reading rather than an explicit equation.

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4; T. Jacobsen, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976); S. N. Kramer, *Sumerian Mythology* (1944/1961); C. Westermann, *Genesis 1-11* (1984); Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004).

terms.translit: šu giri17 ... ĝal2 (hand placed at the nose)
terms.partOfSpeech: Sumerian idiomatic-gesture phrase: hand (šu) + nose (giri17) + place/hold (ĝal2) — obeisance / reverence gesture
terms.literal: they placed / held their hand(s) at their nose(s)
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'did obeisance to him' (functional, gesture dropped); the literal idiom 'hand to the nose' = the Mesopotamian reverence-gesture (Akkadian appa labānu / qāta tabālu)
terms.wohChoice: 'laid their hands upon their noses (in obeisance)' — the literal gesture preserved with a functional gloss; this is a sibling idiom of the central prostration entry giri-ki-su-ub-appa-labanu-prostration-gesture-cross-corpus (which covers the nose-to-the-GROUND prostration; this entry covers the hand-to-NOSE salute).
terms.rationale:
**At line 23 the Anuna gods 'place their hands at their noses' (*šu-bi giri17-ba ... ĝal2*) — the Mesopotamian gesture of obeisance and reverence.** The idiom is *šu* ('hand') + *giri17* ('nose') + *ĝal2* ('to place, to hold'): the worshipper raises the hand to the nose / face in a salute of submission before a superior. ETCSL renders functionally ('did obeisance to him'), dropping the gesture; the WoH translation preserves the literal gesture and adds a parenthetical functional gloss, matching the project's standing preference for keeping the concrete body-language visible.

**Relation to the central prostration entry.** This is a *sibling* gesture, not the same lemma, of the central entry `giri-ki-su-ub-appa-labanu-prostration-gesture-cross-corpus`. That entry covers *giri17 ki su-ub* — pressing the **nose to the ground** in full-body prostration (Sumerian *giri17 ki su-ub*; Akkadian *appa labānu*; Hebrew *šaḥah ʾappayim ʾarṣah*). The present line-23 idiom is the **hand-to-the-nose** salute (a standing or kneeling gesture of reverence, less than full prostration), the Sumerian counterpart of the Akkadian *qāta tabālu* / *labān appi* hand-and-nose gesture-cluster. The two belong to the same Mesopotamian reverence-gesture family (the *nose* — *giri17* / *appu* — is the focal body-part in both), and the cross-corpus body-part-metonymy documented at the central entry applies here too; this overlay entry records the hand-to-nose variant specifically and cross-references the central prostration entry for the fuller comparative apparatus.

**The claim_type is *direct*.** The gesture-idiom is explicit in the Sumerian (hand, nose, place) and the reverence-function is the consensus reading; no contested philology and no WoH-distinctive synthesis is involved.

**Bibliography.** PSD s.v. *giri17*; CAD A/2 pp. 188-189 (*appa labānu*) and CAD L (*labānu*); M. Civil, 'The Sumerian Flood Story' (1969), p. 137 n. 6, on the Sumerian-Akkadian gesture-parallels; D. Gruber, *Aspects of Nonverbal Communication in the Ancient Near East* (1980), on the hand-to-nose / hand-to-mouth reverence gestures; ETCSL c.5.5.4; central entry `giri-ki-su-ub-appa-labanu-prostration-gesture-cross-corpus`.

terms.partOfSpeech: divine name / epithet (birth-goddess): 'Lady of the Crown / Diadem'
terms.literal: Lady of the Crown / Diadem (nin 'lady' + men 'crown/diadem')
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'Ninmena' (preserved); identified by Sumerologists with the birth-goddess (Nintur / Ninhursaĝa / Ninmaḫ) in her crowning-of-the-king aspect
terms.wohChoice: Ninmena (preserved as given); identified in commentary as an epithet of the birth-goddess cluster covered centrally by nintur-nintud-ninhursaga-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster-cross-corpus, in her crown-bestowing / king-making aspect.
terms.rationale:
**Ninmena ('Lady of the Crown / Diadem', *nin* 'lady' + *men* 'crown') sets human reproduction going at line 27** — *^dnin-men-na-ke4 tud-tud al-ĝa2-ĝa2* ('Ninmena set going the begetting of mankind'), having just been described (line 26) as the one who gives birth to lady, en-priest, and king. The name is preserved as given (per the proper-name convention, applied in the chapter). The question for the Editor was whether Ninmena folds into the central birth-goddess epithet-cluster entry, which lists Nintur / Nintud / Ninhursaĝa / Ninmaḫ / Aruru / Mami but does **not** name Ninmena.

**Decision: Ninmena is an epithet of the same birth-goddess function, recorded here (overlay) rather than added to the central cluster.** Ninmena ('Lady of the Crown') is identified in the Sumerological literature with the mother-goddess in her *crown-bestowing / king-making* aspect — the birth-goddess who not only fashions humankind but legitimates kingship by giving birth to (and crowning) the king. The *men* ('crown/diadem') in her name ties directly to line 26's birthing of the *en* (en-priest) and *lugal* (king) and to the 'shining crown' (*men kug*) of line 17. The identification with the birth-goddess cluster (Nintur / Ninhursaĝa / Ninmaḫ) is the consensus: see **Wiggermann**, *RlA* 9, s.v. *Nin-ḫursaĝ*, on the epithet-proliferation of the birth-goddess; **Jacobsen**, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976), pp. 104-110, on the mother-goddess's king-making function; **Krebernik**, *RlA* on the Sumerian birth-goddess names. The reason for **not** promoting Ninmena into the central cluster entry is that Ninmena is a localized epithet here (it does not yet recur across the active corpus the way Nintur / Ninmaḫ / Ninhursaĝa do); the overlay records the identification and cross-references the central entry, which is the project's standard handling for a single-text epithet of an already-centrally-clustered divine function.

**The claim_type is *inferred*.** That Ninmena means 'Lady of the Crown' is direct; that she *is* the birth-goddess (= the Nintur / Ninhursaĝa / Ninmaḫ function) under a crown-aspect epithet is a scholarly identification (consensus, but an identification across names rather than an explicit equation in this text).

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4; F. A. M. Wiggermann, *RlA* 9, s.v. *Nin-ḫursaĝ*; T. Jacobsen, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976); M. Krebernik, *RlA* on the birth-goddess panoply; central entry `nintur-nintud-ninhursaga-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster-cross-corpus`.

terms.partOfSpeech: divine epithet (of Enlil): 'the Honoured / Authoritative One'
terms.literal: the one of authority / the honoured one (an epithet of Enlil)
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL: 'Nunamnir' (preserved); universally identified by Sumerologists as an epithet / by-name of Enlil
terms.wohChoice: Nunamnir (preserved as given); identified in commentary as an Enlil-epithet (= the Enlil of the cosmic triad covered by an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus). Not promoted into the central triad entry's name-list, which fixes on Nudimmud (the Enki epithet); recorded here as a single-text Enlil by-name.
terms.rationale:
**Nunamnir is a standard epithet / by-name of Enlil,** here heading line 28 as 'the leader (*mas-su*) of heaven and earth, Lord Nunamnir' — the one who names the rightful persons and recruits them to provision the gods (lines 28-31). The identification of Nunamnir with Enlil is **uncontested** across the Sumerological literature: Nunamnir is one of Enlil's most frequent literary by-names, especially in Nippur theology (e.g. the *Enlil hymn* / *Enlil in the E-kur*, where Enlil and Nunamnir alternate freely as subject). See **Jacobsen**, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976), pp. 98-104; **Kramer**, *The Sumerians* (1963), pp. 118-122; **Black et al.** (2004), p. 320 (the Enlil-hymn) and p. 309 (the hoe-hymn). The epithet appears to mean something like 'the authoritative / honoured one' (the etymology is debated but the referent is not).

**Decision: identify Nunamnir = Enlil in commentary; do not add to the central triad entry's name-list.** The central entry `an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus` (applied in the chapter) fixes on *Nudimmud* as the relevant epithet (the Enki / fashioner by-name) and treats An-Enlil-Enki as the cosmic triad; Nunamnir is an *Enlil* by-name and is recorded here in the overlay as a single-text epithet, cross-referencing the central triad entry for the Enlil identification. Because the Nunamnir = Enlil equation is uncontested, the claim_type is *direct*. (Contrast Ninmena above, whose identification with the birth-goddess function is an identification-across-names and so *inferred*; Nunamnir = Enlil is a fixed, lexicon-level by-name equation.)

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4; T. Jacobsen, *The Treasures of Darkness* (1976); S. N. Kramer, *The Sumerians* (1963); Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004); central entry `an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus`.

terms.lemma: al-ti-ri2-gu7; dur10-al-lub; sa-al-ḫub2; ma-al-tum; ma-a-a-al-tum; ar-gibil2; al-la-nu-um; ar-ga-nu-um; algameš; al-ĝar-sur9; KI.KAL
terms.partOfSpeech: catalogue of technical / lexicalised nouns, mostly al-initial or hoe-adjacent (bird, axe, net, bowl, sledge, rack, oak, balm/conifer, stone, instrument, grass); several flagged uncertain in ETCSL
terms.standardEnglish: ETCSL transliterates each with a tentative gloss (e.g. 'altirigu bird', 'dur-allub battle-axe', 'maltum bowl', 'mayaltum sledge', 'argibil cupboard', 'allanum oak', 'arganum balm', 'algameš steatite'); several carry (?) in the source token-glosses
terms.wohChoice: Transliterate each technical noun and append the best available gloss ('the al-tirigu bird', 'the dur-allub battle-axe', etc.); preserve the logographic ^u2KI.KAL in capitals per the source; keep the al-gar-sur instrument with its source gloss 'drumsticks'. The /al/ pun in the al-initial members is carried by the parenthetical convention.
terms.rationale:
**Lines 83-93 (with line 51 and lines 71-72) close the hymn with an encyclopedic catalogue of *al*-initial or hoe-adjacent technical nouns,** the paronomasia spilling from the verb-system into the lexicon: in heaven the *al-ti-ri2-gu7* bird (83, glossed 'wren?'); on earth the hoe as dog and dragon (84); on the battlefield the *dur10-al-lub* battle-axe (85); at the city wall the *al-lu5-ḫab2* / *sa-al-ḫub2* battle-net (86); on the table the *ma-al-tum* bowl (87); in the chariot-shed the *ma-a-a-al-tum* sledge (88); in the donkey-stable the *ar-gibil2* rack (89); on the hill-country the *al-la-nu-um* oak (91), the *ar-ga-nu-um* balm/conifer (92), and the *algameš* stone (93); plus the *al-ĝar-sur9* instrument (71-72, source-gloss 'drumsticks') and the logographic *^u2KI.KAL* grass (51).

**These are composition-singular technical lexemes, several explicitly uncertain in the source.** The ETCSL token-glosses themselves carry hedges ('wren?', 'type of net', 'type of bowl', 'type of sledge', 'wooden structure', 'type of conifer', 'type of stone'), and the *al-ĝar-sur9* organology is debated (the *al-ĝar* is elsewhere a stringed/percussion instrument of the gods; the *surx* sign is given with the complex value UZ3×BALAĜ in the source). The WoH translation **transliterates each technical noun and appends the best available gloss**, mirroring ETCSL and preserving the auditability of the uncertain identifications; the logographic *KI.KAL* is kept in capitals per the source (a writing for a type of grass, not securely vocalised). Translating the glosses only ('a bird', 'a bowl') was rejected because it would erase both the /al/ pun and the lexeme that the pun turns on; marking every member with (?) was rejected as cluttering the verse (the uncertainty is recorded here and in commentary instead).

**Why one catalogue entry, not eleven.** Per the project's one-entry-per-lexical-decision principle, these are bundled into a single catalogue entry because they share one rendering-decision (transliterate-plus-gloss, paronomasia-marked) and none recurs across the corpus; individual central entries would be warranted only if any of these lexemes reappears in a later composition. The *al-tirigu* bird and *allanum* oak in particular are *al*-initial by accident of phonology, which is precisely the point of the closing catalogue — the scribe is harvesting the lexicon for the hoe-syllable.

**The claim_type is *inferred*.** The transliteration is direct, but the glosses are tentative (the source itself hedges several), so the rendering-decisions rest on the best-available but non-final identifications — an *inferred* status that flags the lexeme-identifications as provisional for the Reviewer.

**Bibliography.** ETCSL c.5.5.4 token-glosses; Black et al., *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* (2004), pp. 311-312 and notes; PSD / ePSD2 entries for the individual lexemes where available; on the *al-ĝar* instrument, A. D. Kilmer, *RlA* s.v. *Musik* and *Leier/Harfe*.
